title: Optimization of glass separating funnels for microplastic extraction from sediments
author: Wazne, Mermillod-Blondin, et al.

steps.title: Prepare polyamide fragments
steps.instruction: Produce dyed PA particles sized 250–1000 µm for spiking.

substeps.instruction: Acquire polyamide (PA) pellets (Resinex Ltd.) and freeze at –80 °C for 72 h.
Pulverize frozen pellets with liquid nitrogen for 20 min in a Fritsch Pulverisette 0 ball mill.
Sieve the resulting powder with stainless‑steel sieves, retaining particles >250 µm and <1000 µm.
Inspect particle size and shape using a Keyence VHX‑7000 digital microscope with VHX‑7020 camera and VH‑ZST lens.
Stain particles with Nile Red solution (>0.01 mg ml⁻¹) and incubate overnight.
Oven‑dry stained particles at 55 °C for 48 h.

steps.title: Characterize and treat sediment
steps.instruction: Determine sediment grain size and organic matter content before spiking.

substeps.instruction: Collect streambed sediment at Canal de Miribel (45°48′14.2″N 4°53′50.4″E).
Treat three replicate sediment subsamples with ultrasound (50–60 Hz, 1 min) to disperse aggregates.
Measure particle‑size distribution using a Mastersizer 2000 laser granulometer.
Quantify organic matter by loss‑on‑ignition: dry sample 48 h at 55 °C, then combust at 550 °C for 5 h.

steps.title: Create spiked sediment replicates
steps.instruction: Add a known number of PA fragments to dry sediment to achieve 500 particles kg⁻¹ DW.

substeps.instruction: Weigh 30 g dry‑weight sediment for each replicate (seven replicates total).
Count 15 dyed PA fragments under a Nikon SMZ1270 stereo microscope and add them to each 30 g sediment sample.
Mix thoroughly to obtain a uniform spiking concentration of 500 particles kg⁻¹ DW.

steps.title: Dry sediment and add ZnCl₂
steps.instruction: Prepare sediment‑ZnCl₂ mixtures in glass separating funnels.

substeps.instruction: Oven‑dry the spiked sediment matrices for 2 days (48 h) at 55 °C.
Place each dried sediment sample into a 500 mL glass conical separating funnel that already contains ~100 mL ZnCl₂ solution (density 1.5 g cm⁻³).
Add ZnCl₂ solution until the funnel volume reaches ~200 mL.
Gently agitate and shake the funnel several times to homogenize sediment with the dense solution.
Allow the mixture to settle undisturbed for 24 h.

steps.title: Separate sediments using Mohr clamp
steps.instruction: Remove settled sediment without disturbing floating microplastics.

substeps.instruction: Gently open the Mohr clamp attached to the silicone tube at the funnel base to release precipitated sediment.
Move the clamp upward to let sediment exit the tube, or downward to block sediment, regulating discharge and avoiding turbulence.
Drain the sediment through the silicone tube, leaving PA particles and organic matter suspended in the ZnCl₂ solution.
Pour the suspension onto a 63 µm mesh.
Rinse the funnel three times with ultrapure water pre‑filtered through Whatman GF/D glass‑fiber filters (2.7 µm pore size, 47 mm diameter) to collect remaining particles.

steps.title: Collect particles and perform digestion
steps.instruction: Transfer particles to beakers and digest organic material.

substeps.instruction: Transfer the material retained on the 63 µm mesh into a beaker using 50–100 mL of 30 % H₂O₂.
Add 0.05 M Fe(II) solution to the beaker in a 10:1 mL proportion (10 mL water per 1 mL Fe(II) solution).
Incubate the mixture for 24 h to allow digestion of organic matter.

steps.title: Filter digested sample and count particles
steps.instruction: Recover and enumerate PA particles after digestion.

substeps.instruction: The following day, pour the digested suspension through a 63 µm mesh again.
Rinse the mesh with filtered ultrapure water into clean beakers.
Filter the final suspension onto Whatman GF/D glass‑fiber filters (2.7 µm pore size, 47 mm diameter).
Count recovered PA particles under a Nikon SMZ1270 stereo microscope (bright‑field mode, fluorescence not required).

description: In this work, we build on existing devices for extracting microplastics from sediments; by introducing technical adjustments to the commonly used conical shape separating funnels that will allow for easier device manipulation and yield high microplastic recovery rates. These adjustments were made in order to improve the overall efficiency of the microplastic extraction process. To validate if the proposed modifications to the separation funnel design will help enhancing the handling of the manipulation with the glass separation funnels and thus obtain a sufficiently high rate of microplastic recovery, a simple but efficient test was undertaken: First, polyamide (PA) pellets were acquired (Resinex Ltd., High Wycombe, United Kingdom), frozen at −80°C for 72 h, and then pulverized with liquid nitrogen for 20 min in a Fritsch Pulverisette 0 ball mill to form PA fragments. Then using stainless steel sieves, the resultant PA powder was sieved to retain particles smaller than 1000μm and bigger than 250µm. After confirming the size and shape of the PA particles using a digital microscope (Keyence VHX-7000), coupled with a Keyence VHX-7020 camera connected to a Keyence VH-ZST lens (Fig. 2.A), the particles were dyed with high concentrations of Nile Red (> 0.01mg ml−1) overnight and then oven-dried at 55°C for 48 h (Fig. 2.B), yielding fragments of PA that can be easily identified and recovered at the end of the experiment.Fig. 2Particles of polyamide fragments observed under a digital microscope (A), and then colored with Nile Red (B).Fig 2 In a second step, samples of streambed sediment were taken at the Canal de Miribel on the Rhône River in the South-East of France (45°48′14.2″N 4°53′50.4″E). The particle size distribution of the sediment was determined using a laser granulometer (Mastersizer, 2000, Malvern Instrument) on three replicate samples previously treated with ultrasounds (50–60Hz, 1 min) to eliminate non-stable particle aggregates [1].
